It Takes One to Know One: Kevin Chapman

TrueSport

Why this is here: An expert conversation connecting thoughts, physical feelings and behaviour.

Focus on this: Find one example of a thought, one body response and one action. You can read the publisher’s transcript instead.

Open video page ↗Publisher transcript ↗

Keep the distinction: This clip is an application of the stress-process lesson, not a presentation of its exact four-stage model. Nervousness is not compulsory for good performance.

After: Trace one missed serve through demand → appraisal → response → behaviour. Then change the appraisal without changing the score. Which realistic resource or action supports the new thought?

If unavailable: Use the written lesson and the quick explanation below. No video is required.

Inverted-U theory

Oak National Academy

Why this is here: A school-level video lesson explaining an arousal–performance graph.

Focus on this: Open the page’s lesson video. Focus on the axes, the rising part of the curve and the falling part. Extra quizzes and downloads are not assigned.

Open video page ↗

Keep the distinction: This UK lesson covers the Inverted-U, not all the models in Phase 1. Its simplified middle peak is not everyone’s ideal level.

After: Explain why the Inverted-U drawing does not tell every athlete to aim for the same middle number. Contrast that with the individual state-anxiety range described by IZOF.

If unavailable: Use the written lesson and the quick explanation below. No video is required.

Amro Elgeziry on Performance Anxiety

TrueSport

Why this is here: An athlete’s account of expectations, pressure and returning attention to the process.

Focus on this: Look for an expectation about results and a shift toward preparation or the next task. The transcript is on the same page.

Open video page ↗Publisher transcript ↗

Keep the distinction: A personal account illustrates an idea; it does not prove the Catastrophe model or show that the same routine works for everyone.

After: Replace “These nerves mean I will fail” with a statement that acknowledges the demand, names a real resource and gives the athlete one useful next action.

If unavailable: Use the written lesson and the quick explanation below. No video is required.

Kevin Chapman on Performance Anxiety

TrueSport

Why this is here: An expert discussion of evaluation, expectations and pressure around performance.

Focus on this: Identify something about the situation and something about the meaning the athlete gives it. A transcript is available on the publisher page.

Open video page ↗Publisher transcript ↗

Keep the distinction: Some discussion is addressed to adults and uses clinical language. Use the course’s everyday examples, not diagnostic labels for classmates.

After: Describe one situational source and one personal interpretation in a fictional case. Identify one response that changes the situation or obtains support, rather than only changing a thought.

If unavailable: Use the written lesson and the quick explanation below. No video is required.

3 Things to Avoid Saying When It Comes to Body Image

TrueSport · Melissa Streno

Why this is here: An example of how comments around sport can add pressure about appearance.

Focus on this: Read the opening and section 1 on encouragement/advice. Consider a respectful response to a fictional comment; the other sections are optional.

Open reading ↗

Keep the distinction: Do not rate your body or a classmate’s body. You may instead use the uncertainty-about-a-tryout case. The article discusses body image and eating concerns.

After: Describe one situational source and one personal interpretation in a fictional case. Identify one response that changes the situation or obtains support, rather than only changing a thought.

If unavailable: Use the written lesson and the quick explanation below; it contains the teaching needed for this phase.

Practicing relaxation with Progressive Muscle Relaxation

Hertfordshire Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust

Why this is here: An optional demonstration of a structured muscle-relaxation technique.

Focus on this: Watch to explain the difference between structured PMR and a quick reminder to release unnecessary tension. Physical participation is not required.

Open video page ↗

Keep the distinction: Do not tense an injured area, force movements or continue through pain. Use individual professional guidance where relevant.

After: Choose a fictional athlete who is tense and rushing. Explain when a gentle breathing pause might fit, what cue comes next and what would make you stop or change the tool. Contrast this with a flat athlete.

If unavailable: Use the written lesson and the quick explanation below. No video is required.

Principles of Effective Goal Setting

Association for Applied Sport Psychology · Eva V. Monsma

Why this is here: A practitioner’s guide to making goals clear, practical and reviewable.

Focus on this: Read points 1, 2, 4 (the paragraph, not the example table) and 10. Focus on a specific action, review date and strategy.

Open reading ↗

Keep the distinction: The example table does not cleanly match this course’s goal-type distinctions. Use our definitions and SMART wording for assessed work; no public goal chart is required.

After: Write one instructional cue and one motivational cue for a fictional performer. Then turn “perform better” into a SMART process goal, using your existing goal response.
